turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (NURSE): come on back. I'll grab a couple numbers before dr. patel steps in.
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): ok. um. sorry, the parking lot had me going in circles.
[SEG0003] person_1 (NURSE): ha, that lot eats people's mornings. you're alright.
[SEG0004] person_1 (NURSE): blood pressure is 118 over 76, heart rate 78, temp thirty six point eight, oxygen sat 98 percent.
[SEG0005] person_1 (NURSE): my sister had a miserable itch last winter, her little boy too, and folks blamed her housekeeping. drove her nuts.
[SEG0006] person_2 (PATIENT): oh. yeah. I don't know.
[SEG0007] person_3 (DOCTOR): hi, I'm dr. patel. those numbers look steady. what brought you in?
[SEG0008] person_2 (PATIENT): the itching. between my fingers, and right where my jeans sit on my waist. it's driving me nuts.
[SEG0009] person_3 (DOCTOR): itching between the fingers and along the waistband. when did that start?
[SEG0010] person_2 (PATIENT): I don't know, doctor. maybe two weeks, could be three. I can't pin the day down. and it's way worse at night, I wake up scratching.
[SEG0011] person_3 (DOCTOR): roughly two or three weeks, no clear start, worse at night. anybody else at home itching?
[SEG0012] person_2 (PATIENT): my partner, and our little boy. he's four. they're both scratching. we all live in the same apartment.
[SEG0013] person_3 (DOCTOR): partner and your four year old, same apartment, both scratching. what have you put on the rash?
[SEG0014] person_2 (PATIENT): um some hydrocortazone cream, the one percent from the drugstore. used it a few days. didn't really help, so I stopped.
[SEG0015] person_3 (DOCTOR): over the counter hydrocortisone one percent for a few days, then stopped, not much help. anything else you take regularly?
[SEG0016] person_2 (PATIENT): just vitamin d. a thousand units, I think, once a day. the bottle's at home, so I don't know, doctor.
[SEG0017] person_3 (DOCTOR): vitamin d, about a thousand units daily, and you're unsure of the number. any allergies to medicines?
[SEG0018] person_2 (PATIENT): I don't know, doctor. years ago some pill gave me a rash. I can't remember what it was called.
[SEG0019] person_3 (DOCTOR): a rash from a pill you can't name. we won't guess. have you had any fever with this?
[SEG0020] person_2 (PATIENT): mm, I suppose. sometimes, not really.
[SEG0021] person_3 (DOCTOR): I'll leave fever as a maybe, not a yes. any cough, or trouble breathing?
[SEG0022] person_2 (PATIENT): no. nothing like that.
[SEG0023] person_3 (DOCTOR): and your stomach? nausea, diarrhea?
[SEG0024] person_2 (PATIENT): no. stomach's been fine.
[SEG0025] person_3 (DOCTOR): joint pains, or swelling in the hands?
[SEG0026] person_2 (PATIENT): uh, no.
[SEG0027] person_3 (DOCTOR): any blood tests you remember?
[SEG0028] person_2 (PATIENT): last spring they did cholesterol. they said it was borderline. I don't know the actual number. I never went back.
[SEG0029] person_3 (DOCTOR): cholesterol called borderline last spring, no number, not followed up. let me look at your hands and your waist.
[SEG0030] person_3 (DOCTOR): scratch marks in the finger webs, a few small bumps along the waist. no pus, and no big blisters.
[SEG0031] person_2 (PATIENT): is it bad? I don't know, doctor.

[SEG0032] person_3 (DOCTOR): I think this is scabies. a tiny mite burrows in the top layer of skin, and the itch is your body reacting to that mite. that's why it flares at night, and why people in the same home get it together.
[SEG0033] person_2 (PATIENT): scabies? that sounds dirty. I don't know.
[SEG0034] person_3 (DOCTOR): it isn't about being dirty. it spreads by close skin contact and by sharing bedding.
[SEG0035] person_1 (NURSE): mm. my own kid's daycare sent a note about this once, and my sister caught all that shame. wasn't about her floors.
[SEG0036] person_3 (DOCTOR): we'll treat you with permethrin five percent cream. the same night, your partner and your son get treated too, even on skin that isn't itching.
[SEG0037] person_2 (PATIENT): permathrin? I don't know how you even put that on.

[SEG0038] person_3 (DOCTOR): permethrin. tonight, after a cool shower, dry off, then coat every bit of skin from the neck down. between the fingers, under the nails, the waist, the belly button, the groin, the soles. don't skip the creases.
[SEG0039] person_2 (PATIENT): wait, my face too? I don't know, doctor.
[SEG0040] person_3 (DOCTOR): not your face. you're an adult, so neck down is enough. the scalp and face are only for your little boy, and you keep it out of his eyes and mouth.
[SEG0041] person_2 (PATIENT): neck down for me. ok. how long does it stay on?
[SEG0042] person_3 (DOCTOR): eight to fourteen hours. overnight is easiest. wash it off in the morning. then do the exact same thing again in 7 days.
[SEG0043] person_2 (PATIENT): and they do it the same night?
[SEG0044] person_3 (DOCTOR): same night, same routine. the pharmacist can show you how much cream for a four year old.
[SEG0045] person_2 (PATIENT): what about the sheets? do I throw them out? I don't know, doctor.

[SEG0046] person_3 (DOCTOR): don't throw them out. wash the clothes, bedding, and towels from the last three days in hot water and dry them on high. anything you can't wash, seal in a bag for three days. vacuum the couch and the mattress.
[SEG0047] person_2 (PATIENT): hot wash, bags, vacuum. will the itching stop tonight though?

[SEG0048] person_3 (DOCTOR): the mites should die from the cream, but the itch can hang on for two or three weeks while the skin settles. stop the hydrocortisone. I won't add a pill for the itch, because we don't know which pill gave you that rash.
[SEG0049] person_2 (PATIENT): ok. um. do I have to come back?
[SEG0050] person_3 (DOCTOR): yes. I'll have the desk book you in two weeks so I can check the skin again. if it spreads fast, or you see pus, or someone at home gets much worse, call us before that.
[SEG0051] person_1 (NURSE): I can print the cream steps and the laundry list for you on the way out.
[SEG0052] person_2 (PATIENT): thanks. I still feel kind of embarrassed, but alright.

traps.happens: The doctor (or nurse) explains a mechanism or a diagnosis in the patient's body ('the voice box is irritated by reflux', 'diabetes dulls the nerves in the feet', 'the swelling is your body fighting infection'). A nurse or caregiver also mentions a fact about THEIR OWN life (their sister, their child, their own illness).
traps.label_rule: Explanations by the doctor are NEVER symptoms, history or social history of the patient; they may only appear as clinical_assessment or counselling if the doctor stated them as such. A nurse's or caregiver's own life facts are not recorded as the patient's. Each symptom's reported_by is the person who really described it.

features: test_result_recalled: the patient reports an old test or result ('they said it was borderline'); recorded as reported history/investigation only as far as said, not as a confirmed value.
ambiguous_answer: an answer that sounds like yes but is really 'maybe' ('mm, I suppose', 'sometimes, not really'); recorded with uncertainty or not at all, never as a firm fact.
